definition: Grievous means very serious and severe, especially describing harm, injury, or damage.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word grievous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know grievous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: One misplaced decimal in the bridge calculations was a grievous error, forcing engineers to tear out a year of work.
A serious injury demands attention, but a grievous one is graver still — severe and possibly permanent.
Catastrophic harm goes beyond even grievous — total disaster on the largest scale.

Severe means very serious in degree, and it is the standard word across registers: severe weather, a severe sprain, severe delays. Grievous matches that seriousness but is formal and a touch literary, reserved for harm, injury, or wrongdoing described in grave language. A forecast warns of severe storms; a court records grievous bodily harm.

Dire looks forward: dire warnings, dire straits, a dire shortage — the word for a situation threatening disaster ahead and demanding urgent action. Grievous looks back at harm already done and weighs how severe it is: a grievous wound, a grievous error. Dire signals what is coming; grievous measures what has happened.

Grievous means very serious and severe, especially describing harm, injury, or damage.
The night the freighter missed the channel, Keeper Anders rowed out through six-foot swells.
He pulled three sailors from the water, but the second engineer had been thrown against the rocks.
The doctor's telegram to the shipping company did not soften the news: the man's injuries were grievous, and he would never sail again.
Injuries severe enough to end a sailor's career — reported in the gravest possible terms — are what grievous conveys.
Grievous measures the severity of harm rather than naming a specific injury: a deep laceration (another word in this unit) might be grievous, but so can a betrayal or an error — no cut required.
Grievous is also formal and a touch literary; in casual speech, 'serious' usually fits better.
